# Draft:Logistics of the 1868 Republican National Convention

Site selection
By October 1867, the executive committee of the Republican National Committee had begun corresponding with potential host cities for its 1868 presidential nominating convention. https://www.newspapers.com/image/756636665/?match=1&terms=republican%20convention%20to%20be%20held%20in%20chicago https://www.newspapers.com/image/1162310984 On December 11, 1867, during a meeting held at Willard's Hotel in Washington, D.C.., the party's national committeemen formally voted to call for a national convention in Chicago commencing on May 20, 1868. The other competing cities that Chicago beat-out for the opportunity to host the convention were Cincinnati, Ohio; Indianapolis, Indiana; St. Louis, Missouri; and Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

Convention hall preparations
On May 13, the Committee on Arrangements held a meeting where they decided upon a plan of how to modify the convention's main venue, Crosby's Opera House, to serve appropriately as the convention hall. Physical work towards modifying the venue began on May 16.
Plans were adopted to allow approximately 3,600 attendees in the venue at any time. All available space was utilized to accommodate attendees, with the size of the venue limiting furtherer accommodation. The parquet and dress circle sections of the venue were reserved for delegate and alternate delegate seating. This included up to 640 delegates and 300 alternate delegates. The section of seating to the north of the center of the dress circle and extending all the way from the parquet to the building's rear was designated the alternate delegate seating section. Between 1,400 and 1,500 non-delegate spectators were to be admitted in the balcony, family circle, and rear standing room sections. Standing room was also included in the rear of the dress circle for between 400 and 500 spectators. Directly in front of the stage, two rows of work desks for the reporters of local press outlets were placed in the orchestra pit. The rows desks were set up so that half of reporters were seated facing speakers, and the other half were seated facing the delegates.
The stage of the theater was set up to accommodate at least 800 further people during the convention. Convention officers were seated on the stage. The convention president had an assigned desk in the center of the stage, with the convention secretaries having tables immediately beside his desk. Behind the officers, two to three rows of press desks were set up. These desks on the stage including writing facilities for all press writers seeking to keep notes on proceedings, and also featured facilities for the specific needs of out-of-town newspaper correspondents. If needed, further seating for the press were set-up elsewhere on the stage. Behind the rows of desks on the stage, there will be an elevated section erected containing eight raked rows of seating, accommodating 400 to 500 people. This section of seating was to accommodate news editors and visiting political dignitaries. Both wings of the stage featured standing room sections to accommodate approximately 200 further people.
A telegraph office was erected in the theater's south proscenium box. It was installed for use both by the Associated Press (whose reporter would be given a table in front of the box) and for transmission of private dispatches by convention officers.
Coinciding Soldiers' and Sailors' Convention in Chicago
The Soldiers' and Sailors' organization held a convention in Chicago coinciding with the Republican convention. The main session of their convention was held at Turner Hall on May 19, the eve of the Republican convention. That venue was decorated with flags and banners for the event. That convention's Executive Committee rented the Wabash Avenue Rink (a venue with standing room capacity for 6,000 people) to host a grand ratification meeting on May 21.
Similarly, during the 1868 Republican National Convention in July, a coinciding Soliders' and Sailors' convention was held in their convention city.
Hotels
Headquarters hotel: Tremont House
The Tremont House (an establishment with capacity for approximately 1,000 guests) housed the executive membership of the Republican National Committee during the convention.

Soldiers' and Sailors' Convention hotels
Delegates to the coinciding Soldiers' and Sailors' Convention stayed a numerous hotels and boarding houses across the city. The two hotels that accommodated the largest share their delegates were the Briggs House and the Metropolitan Hotel. The Briggs House served as the headquarters of the event's executive committee.
Transit
In order to accommodate any delegates that might opt to stay in Hyde Park rather than downtown Chicago, the Illinois Central Railroad scheduled a special train that would terminate/originate downtown at Great Central Station,  stopping at the 23rd street station and Hyde Park station, as well as all stations located between them.
Tickets and credentials
There was limited availability of tickets.
